AccessToken.description:
Only the access token crosses in the body.

The refresh token goes back as an httpOnly cookie so no script on the page can read
it — including a script injected into the page.
AccessToken.title: AccessToken

AdjustmentCreate.description:
A hand-added line. `reason` is required, not optional.

An unexplained deduction from a final payment is the thing this system exists to
make impossible, so there is no way to add one without saying why.
AdjustmentCreate.title: AdjustmentCreate

DocumentVerify.description: Who checked the paper against the person. A bare boolean would not say.
DocumentVerify.title: DocumentVerify

DueSettlement.description: A settlement against its statutory clock.
DueSettlement.title: DueSettlement

EmployeeSummary.description:
The list row. Deliberately small — an employee list is the highest-traffic
screen in the product and does not need the full record.
EmployeeSummary.title: EmployeeSummary

EmployeeUpdate.description:
Personal details only. Placement changes go through /assignments, and lifecycle
changes through /confirm and /exit, so history cannot be edited away.
EmployeeUpdate.title: EmployeeUpdate

EmploymentType.description: Nepal Labour Act 2074 recognises these employment categories.
EmploymentType.title: EmploymentType

EntitlementsOut.description:
What the frontend may use to decide what to show. Never what the server uses to
decide what to allow — that is `require_module`, on the router.
EntitlementsOut.title: EntitlementsOut

ExitInitiator.description: Who ended the employment. Decides which way notice pay flows.
ExitInitiator.title: ExitInitiator

Headcount.description:
Who works here, cut by one dimension at a time.

`as_of` is recorded on the response because headcount is a point-in-time figure and
a screenshot of one without a date is worthless in a meeting.
Headcount.title: Headcount

HireRequest.description: One call creates the person, their opening assignment and the HIRED event.
HireRequest.title: HireRequest

LeaveTypeUpdate.description: The statutory defaults are unverified, so every one of them is editable.
LeaveTypeUpdate.title: LeaveTypeUpdate

MaritalStatus.description:
Not cosmetic: Nepal's income tax slabs differ for single and married filers, so
payroll reads this in phase 06.
MaritalStatus.title: MaritalStatus

MyDay.description: One day of my own register.
MyDay.title: MyDay

MyLeaveApply.description: No `employee_id`. That is the point of the module.
MyLeaveApply.title: MyLeaveApply

MyPayslipBand.description: `amount` is how much of my income fell in this band; `tax` is what it cost.
MyPayslipBand.title: MyPayslipBand

MyProfile.description:
Who I am, where I sit, and what my employer holds on me.

Deliberately the full record rather than a trimmed one: every field here is the
employee's own personal data, and a person is entitled to see what is stored about
them. The bank account and PAN are theirs. What is *not* here is anyone else's.
MyProfile.title: MyProfile

OfferSent.description:
Returned once, on send.

The token is in the response and in no list endpoint, because it is a credential:
whoever holds it can answer the offer. It goes to the candidate's own link and
nowhere else.
OfferSent.title: OfferSent

OrgUnitKind.description: Depth labels for the single org tree. Ordered broadest to narrowest.
OrgUnitKind.title: OrgUnitKind

OrgUnitNode.description: One node with its subtree, for rendering the chart in a single request.
OrgUnitNode.title: OrgUnitNode

PayrollExportRow.description:
One employee's month, in the shape payroll consumes.

Days, not just minutes: a monthly salary is prorated on days present, while overtime
is paid on minutes. Both are needed, and deriving one from the other loses half-days.
PayrollExportRow.title: PayrollExportRow

PayrollRegisterTotals.description:
What a statutory filing needs, added up once by the server.

The employer's SSF contribution is a cost the company owes on top of gross, not a
deduction from anyone — it is totalled separately so nobody adds it to the wrong
side of a return.
PayrollRegisterTotals.title: PayrollRegisterTotals

Placement.description: Where an employee sits. The same shape whether hiring or moving someone.
Placement.title: Placement

PlanTier.description: The five-tier plan ladder. Also the build order — each tier is roughly a phase.
PlanTier.title: PlanTier

PublicOffer.description:
What a candidate sees at their link.

Deliberately thin. No candidate id, no application id, no requisition code, no
internal notes — a token holder is a candidate, not a user of this system, and
everything beyond the terms they are being asked to accept is the company's.
PublicOffer.title: PublicOffer

RequisitionDetail.description: With the budget it draws against, because that is the question a reader has.
RequisitionDetail.title: RequisitionDetail

RosterAssign.description:
Assign one shift to a set of employees across a date range, in one call.

A roster is filled in a screenful at a time, not row by row — the prototype's
per-row endpoint made a month for forty people four hundred requests.
RosterAssign.title: RosterAssign

StageOutcome.description: What reaching a terminal stage means. Non-terminal stages have none.
StageOutcome.title: StageOutcome

TaxScaleUpdate.description: Replace a scale's bands wholesale, and record who checked them.
TaxScaleUpdate.title: TaxScaleUpdate

UserCreate.description:
Create a login.

The initial password is set by whoever creates the account, which means they know
it. That is the normal shape for HR onboarding and it is not the end state — an
invite-and-set-your-own-password flow is the right answer and is not built yet.
Until it is, this is a deliberate, documented compromise rather than an oversight.
UserCreate.title: UserCreate

UserEmployeeLink.description: Null unlinks. Linking is what opens self-service for this login.
UserEmployeeLink.title: UserEmployeeLink

get.description:
Liveness plus a real database read.

`SELECT 1` is not enough: it needs no table privileges and no schema, so it
answers "connected" for a role that cannot read a single row and for a database
with no tables at all. This once reported a healthy database while every request
was failing with `permission denied for table companies`.

Reading a real table exercises connectivity, privileges and the migrations
together. Unhealthy returns 503, not 200 — a health check that always returns OK
tells a load balancer nothing.

A month of attendance, totalled per employee — phase 04's deliverable to phase 06.

`unlocked_days` is reported rather than hidden: payroll should know it is about to
pay on figures that could still change, and decide whether to lock first.

post.description: Rebuild the daily register for a range. Idempotent; skips locked days.

Approve or reject. Approval writes punches and recomputes the day.

The correction becomes a `regularisation`-sourced punch rather than an edit to the
computed record, so the original device readings survive and the day can still be
rebuilt from scratch.
Assign one shift across employees and dates, replacing anything already there.
Create a login, optionally linked to an employee straight away.

put.description:
Point a login at a person, or unlink it.

Unlinking closes self-service for that login rather than deleting anything — the
leave requests and payslips belong to the employee record, not to the account.

post.description: Create the person, their opening assignment and the HIRED event in one call.

get.description:
Documents that have expired or are about to, soonest first.

The reason `expires_on` is a column. A work permit or a contract that lapses
unnoticed is a compliance problem, and nobody finds it by opening employee records
one at a time.

Already-expired rows are included, with a negative `days_remaining`, because those
are the urgent ones — filtering them out would hide exactly the failures this is
for. Rows with no expiry date are not "never expiring"; they are simply not this
report's subject.

post.description: Transfer, promote or redesignate. Closes the previous assignment.

get.description: Stream the file. Always an attachment — see `documents.py` for why.

post.description:
Attach the actual file to a document record.

Separate from creating the record because the record legitimately exists first:
HR lists what it still needs to collect, and the expiry report is most useful for
exactly those rows.

Mark a document checked, naming the checker.

The verifier is the caller, taken from the token rather than the body. Letting the
request name who verified it would make the field worth nothing.

get.description:
My register for one month, totals included.

A month rather than an arbitrary range: this is the unit an employee checks their
pay against, and an unbounded range on a self-service endpoint is an easy way to
ask the database for ten years of rows.

Download one of my own documents.

Filtered on my employee id as well as the tenant, so a colleague's document id is
indistinguishable from one that does not exist. A self-service download that
checked only the tenant would hand any employee every contract in the company.

post.description:
Apply for my own leave.

Same service call as `POST /leave/requests`, so the overlap check, the half-day
rule and the working-day count are identical — the only difference is where the
employee id comes from, and here it cannot come from the caller.

Withdraw a request of mine that nobody has decided yet.

Only `pending`. Undoing an *approved* leave moves a balance and belongs with the
approver — `POST /leave/requests/{id}/cancel` does that, with the ledger entries it
requires. The id is filtered on the employee as well as the tenant, so a request
that is not mine is a 404 and not a permission error: whether someone else's
request exists is not mine to learn.

get.description: My approved payslips, newest first.

One payslip of mine, itemised down to the tax bands.

The id is filtered on my employee id, not merely checked afterwards, so another
employee's payslip is indistinguishable from one that does not exist.

post.description:
Post accruals. With a month, that month; without one, the whole year.

Idempotent: a second run over the same period posts nothing, because a cron job
eventually runs twice and nobody should get a double entitlement out of it.

get.description: Every movement behind a balance — the answer to "why do I have 11.5 days?".

post.description:
HR raising a request on someone's behalf. `/ess/leave/requests` is the same call
with the employee taken from the token instead of the body.
Cancel approved leave, returning the entitlement as a reversal entry.
Approve or reject. Approval consumes the balance in the same transaction.

get.description: Seeds the statutory catalogue on first read, so a new tenant is never empty.
What the candidate sees. Only the terms they are being asked to accept.

post.description:
Accept or decline.

Accepting also moves the application to the pipeline's hired stage, so the board
and the offer cannot disagree about whether someone was hired.

get.description: The whole chart in one request — one query, assembled in memory, no N+1.
One payslip with every line and every tax band it was built from.

post.description: Approve, and lock the attendance the run was computed from.

get.description: Every salary period, newest first — a raise opens a row, never edits one.
The company's own bands. Seeded from unverified statutory defaults.

put.description:
Replace a scale's bands, and record who checked them.

Naming a verifier is what flips `is_verified`. That is deliberate: "verified" should
mean a person put their name to it, not that someone clicked a box.

get.description:
Ordered by when they arrived.

Not by a score. The prototype sorted this list by an `ai_score` a language model
wrote, which decided who a recruiter looked at first and therefore who got hired.
One application with its whole history — every stage, who moved it, and why.

post.description: Move to another stage. Appends to the history; never overwrites it.

get.description: Never includes `response_token`. It is a credential, not a field.

post.description:
Mark it sent and return the candidate's response token, once.

The token is not in any list endpoint. Whoever holds it can answer the offer, which
makes it a credential — it belongs in the candidate's link and nowhere else.
Raise a requisition against a budgeted position.

Filled, or cancelled. Either way it stops accepting applications and stops
counting against the position's budget.
Approve it, which is what lets applications be taken against it.

get.description: The company's hiring stages. Seeds the default pipeline on first read.

post.description: Add a stage. A hiring process differs between a bank and a construction firm.

get.description:
Who works here, cut one way at a time.

`group_by` is a literal rather than a string, so the set of dimensions is in the
OpenAPI spec, in the generated client, and refused at the edge — not validated
somewhere inside the query builder.
What the company owes in leave, per person per type.

One payroll run as a register, with the totals a filing needs.

Available for a computed run as well as an approved one: the register is how
somebody checks a run *before* approving it, and withholding it until after
approval would make the check impossible.

post.description:
Raise a settlement for someone who has left, and compute it straight away.

Computing on creation rather than leaving it as an empty draft: the fifteen-day
clock starts at the last working day, not at whenever someone remembers to press a
button, so the figures should exist from the moment the record does.

get.description:
Settlements against their statutory clock, most urgent first.

The whole reason `deadline` is a column. An unpaid final settlement is a compliance
failure with a date attached, and nobody finds it by opening leaver records one at a
time. Already-overdue rows come first with a negative `days_remaining` — those are
the ones that matter, and filtering them out would hide the failures this exists for.

post.description: Add a hand-entered line, then recompute so the totals include it.
Approve, consuming the leave it pays out in the same transaction.

Cancel, freeing the employee for a new settlement.

Refused once approved: approving posted encashment rows into the leave ledger, and
a cancel that left them there would show a balance paid out against a settlement
that officially never happened. Reversing them is a decision with money attached
and needs its own deliberate operation rather than a status change.
Recompute from current data. Refused once approved — that is a snapshot.
Record the disbursement date, which is what stops the statutory clock.
